I think the answer is, "it depends". It depends on what the sub wants, and how the sub wants to be run. If the goal of a sub is to have civil discourse about topics, then I think it is quite within the rights of the mods (perhaps even necessary of them) to ban offenders. If the goal is to have free speech, then one simply has to accept the consequences of that - even when they're unfriendly. For default subs on Voat, I think free speech has to be king.

IMO, a better question is this: is it reasonable to punish name-calling etc. towards mods more frequently, more readily, or more severely than towards users? From the perspective of egalitarianism, the answer is clearly "no" - mods are users, and all users should be treated the same. From our real world perspectives, though, this isn't how the world works. People are expected to have respect for office - showing contempt towards a judge or assaulting a police officer is punished more harshly than similar offences towards others in the community. While this may be seen as creating a climate of fear and oppression, it is also useful in ensuring the system functions smoothly. Being in such positions puts one in the crosshairs of those who would reject the law; meanwhile, severity of punishment is a primary discourager of crime (a person will be less willing to commit a crime that would see them jailed for 10 years, vs 30 days). The increased risk and exposure of these members of the community could be seen to warrant the necessity of more severe punishments in order to bring the risk to those in these offices down to the average for the remainder of the community. Without such punishments, it may be difficult to find people willing to fill such positions, and, at the least, the candidates may be sub-optimal. Can this be extended to similar offices and offences in an online community?
